openers.title: The Haber-Bosch Harvest
openers.question: About half the nitrogen in your body passed through a factory. Inside a steel reactor, nitrogen from the air meets hydrogen gas at 500 °C. Ammonia forms. But the reactor never turns all of the gas into ammonia. Some nitrogen and hydrogen are always left over. What are the molecules doing that keeps the reaction from going all the way?
openers.model_answer: Nitrogen and hydrogen molecules collide and react to form ammonia. At the same time, ammonia molecules break apart into nitrogen and hydrogen again. As ammonia builds up, the reverse reaction speeds up and the forward reaction slows. When the two rates are equal, the amounts stop changing, but both reactions keep running. So some nitrogen and hydrogen are always left.
openers.target: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates become equal, amounts stop changing, and the reaction does not go to completion

openers.title: The Martian Fuel Factory
openers.question: Astronauts on Mars will need fuel to fly home. A robot fills a sealed steel chamber with carbon monoxide and steam and heats it to 800 K. Hydrogen fuel starts to form. A gas analyzer shows the hydrogen rising, then holding steady, while some carbon monoxide is still inside. The pressure gauge never moves at all. What are the molecules doing once the analyzer reading stops changing?
openers.model_answer: Carbon monoxide and water molecules collide and swap atoms to make carbon dioxide and hydrogen. At the same time, carbon dioxide and hydrogen molecules collide and swap back. When the two happen at the same rate, the amounts stop changing, but both reactions keep running. Each swap trades two molecules for two, so the number of molecules, and the pressure, never changes.
openers.target: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates become equal, amounts stop changing, and the reaction does not go to completion

openers.title: The Silent Beaker
openers.question: A sealed beaker holds water over a layer of white silver chloride. The solid has sat there for days. A silver-ion probe in the water gives a steady reading. A radiation probe near the top of the water reads 0 counts per minute. Now a chemist drops a small pellet of radioactive silver chloride onto the solid at the bottom. The silver-ion probe does not move. But the radiation count starts to rise, then levels off. The beaker looks as still as before. What microscopic processes are taking place between the solid and the solution?
openers.model_answer: Dissolution and precipitation at equal rates (dynamic equilibrium). Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ leave the lattice and redeposit continuously; [Ag⁺] constant. Tracer ¹¹⁰ᵐAg⁺ exchanges into solution until distributed; count rises, then levels.
openers.target: Dynamic equilibrium in a saturated solution: dissolving and settling go on at equal rates; adding more solid does not change Q.

openers.title: The Purple Piston
openers.question: A sealed glass cylinder at 400 °C holds hydrogen, purple iodine vapor and colorless hydrogen iodide. The mixture has sat for hours. A detector shines green light through the gas and reads how much of it the purple iodine absorbs. Now a motor pushes the piston down and squeezes the gas into half the space. The detector's reading jumps to twice what it was. Then it holds steady, hour after hour. How does compression change the rates of the forward and reverse reactions?
openers.model_answer: Halving V doubles every concentration. Forward rate ∝ [H₂][I₂] rises 4×; reverse rate ∝ [HI]² rises 4×. Rates stay equal; Q = K (Δn = 0); no shift. Absorbance doubles from concentration alone.
openers.target: When the moles of gas are the same on both sides of the equation, a change in volume changes every concentration by the same factor; Q stays equal to K, and nothing shifts.

media.image_alt: A cartoon of a brass and glass cylinder with a piston, full of swirling purple gas. A green light beam crosses the gas toward a detector screen.

openers.title: The Fading Brown
openers.question: A sealed glass cell with a piston sits at 25 °C. A detector shines blue light through it and reads how much light the gas absorbs. Brown nitrogen dioxide absorbs blue light; colorless dinitrogen tetroxide does not. A chemist fills the cell with brown nitrogen dioxide. In a split second the brown fades, and the detector's reading drops. Then the color stops changing. The reading holds steady, hour after hour. What microscopic processes continue once the color is constant?
openers.model_answer: 2NO₂ → N₂O₄ (dimerization) and N₂O₄ → 2NO₂ (dissociation) at equal rates; dynamic equilibrium. [NO₂] constant, so absorbance constant.
openers.target: A steady color does not mean the reaction has stopped: joining and splitting go on at equal rates. Squeezing shifts this equilibrium toward fewer gas molecules; warming shifts it toward the reaction that takes in heat.

table@v:equal.show: Step 2 is the ICE table. Initial: your starting concentrations, and 0 for both products. Change: \(-x\) for CO and H2O, \(+x\) for CO2 and H2, because every coefficient is 1. Equilibrium: initial plus change. Fill in the table.

x_found@v:equal.show: Taking the positive square root gives \(\sqrt{K_c} = \dfrac{x}{[CO]_0 - x}\). Solve that for x. Type x.

other_root_checked@v:equal.show: A square root also has a negative value: \(-\sqrt{K_c} = \dfrac{x}{[CO]_0 - x}\). Solve it, and put that x into the equilibrium row. A root is physically meaningful only if every concentration comes out zero or positive. Say which root the chamber rejects, and why.

leftover_found@v:equal.show: Carbon monoxide at equilibrium is its starting concentration minus x. Type it with M.

expression_set@v:unequal.show: Put the equilibrium row into \(K_c\): \(K_c = \dfrac{x^2}{([CO]_0 - x)([H_2O]_0 - x)}\). This time the two starting concentrations differ. Type it with your numbers.
